title: Genesis 28. The Cup of the Dream.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 28. The Cup of the Dream.
Isaac called Jacob and blessed him and commanded him:
You shall not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan.
Arise, go to Paddan-aram, to the house of Bethuel your mother's father.
Take a wife from there,
from the daughters of Laban your mother's brother.
May God Almighty bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you,
that you may become a company of peoples.
And may He give you the blessing of Abraham,
to you and to your offspring with you,
that you may inherit the land of your sojourning,
which God gave to Abraham.
The blessing is spoken again.
This time knowingly.
In chapter twenty-seven, Isaac was blind and deceived.
Here he sees, not with his eyes, which are still dim,
but with understanding.
He blesses Jacob with the blessing of Abraham.
The Cup that was stolen in goatskin is now given in the open.
The father who trembled now speaks the promise deliberately.
The same words Abraham's servant swore by:
the God of heaven and earth.
The same promise: offspring, land, blessing.
The Cup that passed from Abraham to Isaac now passes from Isaac to Jacob,
not through deception but through a father's final word.
Isaac sent Jacob away.
He went to Paddan-aram, to Laban the son of Bethuel the Syrian,
the brother of Rebekah, Jacob's and Esau's mother.
Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him away.
He saw that Isaac commanded him:
Do not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan.
He saw that Jacob obeyed his father and his mother.
Esau sees.
The brother who was robbed now watches the brother who robbed him receive a second blessing,
this time openly,
this time with a command that matches what Esau failed to do.
Esau married Hittite women.
Jacob is sent to find a wife from the kindred.
The older brother who despised his birthright and married outside the line now sees the younger brother sent to marry inside it.
So Esau went to Ishmael and took Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael,
Abraham's son, the sister of Nebaioth, to be his wife,
in addition to the wives he already had.
Esau tries to please.
He marries a daughter of Ishmael,
the other son who was sent away.
The two cups of arrangement join.
The son who was cast out gives his daughter to the son who was passed over.
But the marriage does not restore the birthright.
The marriage does not return the blessing.
Esau is still outside.
Trying to enter through a door that has already closed.
Jacob went out from Beersheba and went toward Haran.
The same road his grandfather walked, in reverse.
Abraham left Haran for Canaan.
Jacob leaves Canaan for Haran.
The man who carries the Cup is now walking away from the land the Cup promised.
The vessel that holds the promise is running from the land the promise names.
The heir of Beersheba, the well of the oath,
the place of the tamarisk tree,
the place where God appeared as El Olam, leaves it behind.
He came to a certain place and stayed there that night,
because the sun had set.
Taking one of the stones of the place,
he put it under his head and lay down in that place to sleep.
The sun has set.
The man who deceived his father in the dark now lies down in the dark.
No tent.
No bed.
No Rebekah.
No Isaac.
No Esau.
A stone for a pillow.
The ground for a mattress.
The sky for a roof.
The man who grabbed a heel and stole a blessing and invoked God's name in a lie now sleeps on a rock with nothing but what he is carrying,
which is nothing.
He dreamed.
A stairway.
a ladder, a ramp, a staircase.
Set on the earth.
Its top reaching to heaven.
And behold, the angels of God were ascending and descending on it.
The tower of Babel tried to reach heaven by building.
A stairway was built from the ground up, brick by brick,
city by city, name by name.
And God came down to scatter it.
Here a stairway appears that no one built.
It stands on the earth.
It reaches to heaven.
And the traffic on it is not human ambition but divine messengers,
ascending and descending, going up and coming down,
moving between the place where Jacob sleeps and the place where God is.
The tower that could not reach heaven is replaced by a stairway that comes from heaven.
Babel tried to climb.
Bethel receives.
The Cup that was scattered at Babel is now offered to a man sleeping on a stone.
And behold, the Lord stood above it and said:
I am the Lord,
the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac.
The land on which you lie I will give to you and to your offspring.
Your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth,
and you shall spread abroad to the west and to the east and to the north and to the south.
In you and in your offspring all the families of the earth shall be blessed.
Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go,
and will bring you back to this land.
For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.
The covenant, spoken to Abraham in Ur, confirmed by stars in Hebron,
cut in blood at Moriah, sealed in flesh at ninety-nine,
tested on a mountain, sworn by oath, inherited through wells at Beersheba,
now comes to Jacob.
In a dream.
On a stone pillow.
While he is running for his life from the brother he robbed.
God does not wait for Jacob to be worthy.
He comes while Jacob sleeps.
The same God who walked alone through the pieces while Abraham slept now speaks alone from heaven while Jacob sleeps.
The vessel that stole the blessing receives the promise without earning it.
The hand that grabbed a heel, that grabbed a birthright,
that grabbed a blessing, is now open, unconscious, holding nothing.
And God fills it.
The land on which you lie.
Jacob is lying on the promised land.
He does not know it.
He stopped because the sun set.
He chose a stone because he needed a pillow.
He slept because he was tired.
And the ground he is lying on is the ground God is giving him.
The Cup that was promised to Abraham now rests under Jacob's head as a rock.
Your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth.
The same word used with Abraham in chapter thirteen, dust.
The same word used for Abram's body in chapter three,
the dust you shall return to.
What was a sign of death becomes a sign of multitude.
And now it is spoken over a man who has no children,
no wife, no tent, no land in his name.
The vessel that holds the promise of dust countless offspring is lying alone on a rock.
In you and in your offspring all the families of the earth shall be blessed.
The same word spoken to Abraham in chapter twelve.
The same word sworn by oath in chapter twenty-two.
The same word that has echoed through every generation since Ur.
Now spoken to the man who stole it.
The Cup does not ask whether the vessel deserves it.
It asks whether God has chosen it.
Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go,
and will bring you back to this land.
For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.
I will not leave you.
The same God who said to Isaac: I am with you.
The same God who said to Abraham: I am your shield.
Now says to Jacob, the deceiver, the grabber, the runner:
I will not leave you.
The promise does not depart when the vessel runs.
The Cup travels with the one who stole it.
The God who was not consulted in the deception is the God who appears in the dream.
The word that was taken by trickery is now given freely.
Jacob woke from his sleep and said:
Surely the Lord is in this place,
and I did not know it.
He did not know it.
The man who invoked God's name in a lie to his father now discovers that God was in a place he did not name,
did not consecrate, did not choose.
He stopped because the sun set.
He slept because he was tired.
He dreamed because God came.
And he did not know it until he woke.
He was afraid and said: How awesome is this place!
This is none other than the house of God,
and this is the gate of heaven.
The first time fear and awe are joined in one response since Abraham fell on his face at El Shaddai.
Jacob, who calculated risk before deceiving his father,
who assessed the danger of being caught,
now fears for a different reason.
The place is holy.
The ground is holy.
The stone is holy.
The man who tricked his father with goatskin is now standing on ground where heaven and earth touch.
Jacob rose early in the morning and took the stone that he had put under his head and set it up for a pillar and poured oil on the top of it.
He called the name of that place Bethel, of God.
House The stone that was a pillow becomes a pillar.
The stone that held a sleeping head now holds oil.
The same gesture as Abraham planting a tamarisk tree at Beersheba.
The same impulse: to mark the place where God spoke.
But where Abraham planted a living tree,
Jacob sets up a dead stone.
Where Abraham called on El Olam, the Everlasting God,
Jacob names the place the House of God.
The tree grows.
The stone stands.
The Cup is held by both.
But the name of the city was Luz at first.
Luz, almond tree.
The place already had a name.
Jacob renames it.
The man who renamed himself as Esau now renames a city as Bethel.
The deceiver who stole an identity now gives one.
The grabber who took what was not his now marks what was given to him.
Then Jacob made a vow:
If God will be with me and keep me on this way that I go,
and give me bread to eat and clothing to wear,
so that I come again to my father's house in peace,
then the Lord shall be my God.
And this stone, which I have set up for a pillar,
shall be God's house.
And of all that You give me I will give a full tenth to You.
If.
The word hangs in the air.
God said: I am with you.
Jacob says: If God will be with me.
God said: I will keep you.
Jacob says: If He will keep me.
God said: I will bring you back.
Jacob says: If I come again to my father's house in peace.
The promise was unconditional.
The response is conditional.
The Cup was given freely.
The hand that receives it attaches terms.
Jacob's faith starts with if.
The man who has just heard God speak the same covenant He spoke to Abraham and Isaac,
the man who has seen a stairway between earth and heaven,
responds with a contract.
If You do this, then You shall be my God.
If You give me bread and clothing and a safe return,
then I will give You a tenth.
Abraham gave a tithe to Melchizedek without conditions.
Abraham believed God, and it was counted as righteousness.
Isaac built an altar and called on the name of the Lord.
Jacob sets terms.
The Cup of the dream is received,
but the hand holding it isn't sure yet.
The vessel that grabbed everything now asks God to prove Himself before he commits.
But the vow also contains something Abraham and Isaac never said:
This stone shall be God's house.
Jacob marks a place.
Not just an altar.
Not just a tree.
A house.
The man who is running from his father's house names a stone as God's house.
The man who has no home consecrates one.
The vessel that holds the Cup is homeless,
and the first thing he does with the promise is build a dwelling for the One who gave it.
The stairway connected earth and heaven.
The promise came down while Jacob slept.
He did not build it.
He did not climb it.
He did not earn it.
He laid his head on a stone, and God came to him.
The Cup of the dream, full, unconditional, unearned,
is now in the hands of a man who says if.
The God who said I will not leave you is answered by a man who says then you shall be my God.
The gap between what God said and what Jacob said is the gap between grace and bargaining.
The Cup is full.
The hand that holds it is not yet open.
But the dream was real.
The stairway stood.
The voice spoke.
And the man who stole a blessing received one he did not steal.
The Cup holds.
The vessel learns.
Slowly.
